items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: Keith accompanied visiting and emigrating American jazz artists, including Benny Carter and Ben Webster

ctx.x: Well, you have to go back to work soon, but I wanted to follow up quickly on one little thing — you mentioned the thing about The Beatles in ‘64. They certainly changed our society but no one ever said anything about the fact that they opened up a market even for jazz musicians to go over?

Yes they did. I mean it’s not only them but all the groups that came afterwards, I mean Gerry and the Pacemakers and all these groups, they came over to America because they had hit records. And we started to get that. And you could send the pop groups over, and we would get American jazz artists in return. So I mean if you could send a group of four, five guys, you could get, in effect — I mean at the time there weren’t American groups in a way that would go over there. You didn’t have as many. But we had the…

terrificly long shelf life, I think it’s wonderful. But you know we used to get, the musicians would come back. So we’d say good-bye Mick Jagger, hello Ben Webster. Thank God. I’ll settle for that. That’s fair exchange and no robbery. That’s perfect.
